ch01.text: Before the walkthroughs, the concepts, because a consultant who cannot explain the books will lose the client's accountant in the first meeting. Accounting runs on one equation: assets equal liabilities plus equity, and every transaction touches it twice. ERPNext enforces that twice-ness by refusing to save an unbalanced journal entry, which makes the rule visible. There are five account types, and the type decides the report: assets, liabilities and equity on the balance sheet, income and expenses on the profit and loss. Malaysian clients often arrive with a chart built in a spreadsheet, so your job is to map each row to a type, not to impose your own taste. Next, accrual accounting: income when earned, expenses when incurred. Tax collected is never income; it is a liability cleared when you file. Then the three ledgers. The general ledger says what the business earned and owns. The stock ledger says where the goods are and what they cost. The payment ledger says who owes what, document by document. One mistake is often invisible in two of the three, which is why month end reconciles all of them. Control accounts and party ledgers must agree, and you never fix a difference by journaling into debtors. Finally, journals: right for accruals and depreciation, wrong as a replacement for a purchase invoice or a sale. Close with four checks and five questions, because trust is built on numbers that survive scrutiny.

ch02.text: The second primer is distribution, because a distributor earns margin by holding stock and taking risk. Think in three flows. Goods move from supplier to warehouse to customer and sometimes back. Money moves the other way, delayed by the terms you agree. Information, promises and availability, is the flow ERPNext owns. Channels explain why one product has four prices: retail pays list, dealers expect a discount, distributors buy lowest and take stock, exports add currency and freight. Each channel becomes a price list, a customer group and often a warehouse rule. Then margins: selling price less landed cost, where landed cost includes freight and duty. A blender at two hundred forty with a landed cost of one hundred twenty six earns one hundred fourteen, and a ten percent discount takes that to ninety. Positioning is the arithmetic that keeps the business running: demand during lead time plus safety stock. Two units a day for seven days, plus ten, is twenty four, not a round twenty. Fulfilment runs order, availability, pick, ship, invoice, collect, and the delivery note is where stock and cost of goods move. Exceptions are normal: partial shipments, backorders, substitutions, over-deliveries. A commitment is history once submitted, so reduce quantities or raise documents, never edit. Returns need a quarantine policy. The five KPIs are fill rate, on time in full, inventory turns, GMROI and days sales outstanding. In the lab you compute them.

ch03.text: Every ERPNext document has three states, and one hidden field decides which state it is in. A draft is a proposal: you can type anything, save it as often as you like, and nothing happens to stock or to the books. A submitted document is a commitment. The single click writes a stock ledger entry and a general ledger pair, and the document freezes. A cancelled document is history: the postings are reversed by offsetting rows, and the record stays exactly where it was. Nothing is deleted, which is why an auditor can follow a mistake from beginning to end. When something is wrong, cancel first and then amend, because amendment is only offered on a cancelled document and it creates a new one linked back through amended_from. If a cancel is refused, look for the active referencing document and unwind the chain from the bottom, invoice before delivery. And remember what reports read: only submitted records. A hundred draft invoices are invisible to receivables ageing. Teach the five minute demo, draft, submit, cancel, amend, and most objections never get raised.

ch04.text: Operators lose more time finding things than typing them, so Volume zero continues with the interface itself. One search box at the top of the Desk reaches every DocType, every document, every report and a set of commands, which is faster and more durable than memorising a menu tree that moves between versions. The list view is the real interface: filters that stack, columns you choose, sorting by modified date, a record count at the bottom, and selection checkboxes that unlock bulk actions and exports. Take a filter combination that answers a real question, name it for the job, set it as the default for a role, and you have built a work queue that costs nothing to maintain and survives every upgrade. Remember that saved filters are shared while user permissions narrow the rows, so always test a view as the person who will use it. For anything needing joins or logic, Report Builder stops and a Script Report begins, and that is a decision to write down, because it becomes something you support.

ch05.text: Welcome to the consultant track. This course is not about how ERPNext is built; it is about standing it up for a client, entering real data and proving the result to the sen. Volume zero starts with the company. Every account name carries the company abbreviation, so choose the two letters before you save. Country selects the chart of accounts template, currency is effectively fixed after the first transaction, and the fiscal year decides which period your postings land in. Then you verify, not the form, but the result: five root groups, every account ending in your abbreviation, a debtors control account, and the company selectable in global defaults. Next, add the accounts your client actually needs: petty cash, freight inward, and two tax accounts, one for sales tax and one for service tax, both flagged as tax accounts. Group accounts never take postings, and ERPNext refuses the voucher. Defaults come next: round off, write off, default cost centre and default warehouse. They look cosmetic, and they pre-fill every document. Then cost centres, built around how the client makes decisions, with a check that the columns add up to the total. Finally Malaysian SST: item tax templates for ten percent goods and eight percent services, a document template on net total, and a test invoice that must show one thousand two hundred net, one hundred twenty tax, and one thousand three hundred twenty payable. In the lab you build it and record every choice.

ch06.text: Volume zero, second half: making the system usable. Start with units. A unit is master data, and a conversion factor is the contract between buying and selling. If the client buys boxes of twelve and sells pieces, you need both units and the factor of twelve before the first receipt, because stock is valued in the stock unit and history cannot be rewritten afterwards. Test it: one box must post twelve pieces, and half a box must be refused. Next, warehouses. Each location points at a stock account, so main stock, retail counter, assembly floor and returns quarantine are four warehouses with one default. Transfer five units and the company total must not move. Then users. A user is a login, a role is a bundle of permissions, and a role profile is a reusable bundle of roles. Create named users, because shared logins destroy the audit trail, and always demonstrate the restricted login rather than the administrator, who bypasses everything. Permissions have two layers: roles decide verbs such as create, submit and cancel, while user permissions decide rows, for example a storekeeper seeing only the main warehouse. Naming series are a contract with the auditor, so agree the format, then test it on a draft. Finally settings: FIFO valuation, negative stock off, credit limit on, default warehouse and price list. Volume zero ends with a ten point handover sheet signed by the client, because a foundation nobody approved is an argument waiting to happen.

ch07.text: Volume one is the item master, and items are where costing decisions wear product names. Start with item groups. They are a reporting tree, so group by commercial family, not by supplier, and keep it three levels deep. Then a complete stock item. Maintain stock decides whether the item touches inventory at all. Valuation rate is a cost, not a price, and putting the selling price there ruins every margin report from day one. The default unit drives buying and selling, the income and expense accounts decide where sales and cost of goods post, and the item tax template attaches tax to the product rather than the invoice. Next, tracking. Serial numbers identify individual units and suit warranty appliances; batches group production runs and suit packaging with expiry. Both flags must be set before the first stock movement, because history cannot be retracked. A service item has maintain stock off, so it never appears in stock reports. Only track what the business genuinely needs to trace, and ask for one process that depends on it. Finally, prices and reorder rules. Item price records hold a rate per price list and per date, so a price change is history rather than an edit. Reorder level needs safety stock and lead time to be useful. And remember the zero-rate trap: if a quotation shows zero, a price record is missing, not a system bug. In the lab you build five items across all three types and prove the price and tax behaviour.

ch08.text: Volume one, part two: parties and pricing. A customer record is a set of defaults plus two controls. The group and territory organise reporting. The price list and payment terms decide behaviour. The credit limit is the only thing that stops a sale, and it lives in the customer's credit limits table, which is why the sample company sets five thousand here; a later lesson sells six thousand and must be blocked. Payment terms belong on the customer so every invoice inherits them; typing terms per invoice is how one customer ends up with three due dates. Then addresses, which are separate records linked to the customer. Mark one as primary billing, one as primary shipping, add a contact, and check the printed document rather than the form. Completeness matters now, because state and postcode are optional for a PDF and mandatory for an e-Invoice. Suppliers are simpler but the terms drive cash flow: thirty days here, fourteen there, and the payment proposal becomes useful instead of decorative. Finally pricing, which has two layers. An item price is a fact for a price list and a date. A pricing rule is a calculation applied when conditions match. The customer's price list picks the facts, then the rule adjusts them. Ten blenders for a dealer at two hundred sixteen, less five percent, is two hundred five ringgit twenty. Nine units is two hundred sixteen, because the minimum quantity is not met. Predict the number before you open the quotation; that is the consultant's habit.

ch09.text: Volume two is the transaction chain, and this is the heart of consultant training: five documents, three ledgers, and numbers you predict before you press submit. A quotation writes nothing but an offer. It carries the customer's price list, terms and tax, and when it is submitted the general ledger stays empty and stock does not move. A sales order is a commitment. It still posts nothing, but projected quantity falls by five, delivery dates and warehouses are set per line, and the order becomes the source for delivery and billing. The delivery note is where stock finally moves. Five units leave the main warehouse at a valuation of one hundred twenty each, so cost of goods sold is six hundred, and the order says fully delivered. Still no receivable. The sales invoice posts three things at once: debtors one thousand three hundred twenty, revenue one thousand two hundred, and SST payable one hundred twenty. Gross profit becomes six hundred, a fifty percent margin. Then the payment entry. Receive one thousand three hundred twenty into the bank, allocate it to the invoice, and the invoice turns paid and the payment ledger returns to zero. An unallocated receipt is the most common cause of a wrong aged receivables report, so always allocate. In the lab you run the whole cycle and then prove it with three reports: general ledger, payment ledger and gross profit.

ch10.text: Volume two, second half: what happens when reality intervenes. Partial delivery first. Do not split the order; reduce the delivery quantity against the same order. Two of five units moves stock by two, posts cost of goods of two hundred forty, and leaves the order at forty percent delivered and forty percent billed, still open for the rest. Next, discounts. A line discount of ten percent on one thousand two hundred gives one thousand eighty net, one hundred eight tax and one thousand one hundred eighty eight total, while cost stays six hundred, so gross profit falls to four hundred eighty. Tax follows taxable value, and learners who expect the tax to stay at one hundred twenty will misquote a customer. Then returns. A credit note is three reversals in one document: stock comes back, revenue is reversed through sales return, and the tax is reversed too. One unit at two hundred forty reverses twenty four of tax and credits the customer two hundred sixty four, and because it is created against the original invoice, the link survives an audit. Never create a negative-priced invoice. Credit limits are the one setting that stops an order. Enable credit checking in selling settings, set a five thousand limit, and a six thousand order will not submit. Blocking at submit, not at save, is deliberate. Finally, close the month with four reports and an exception list where every difference has a name against it. In the lab you break, correct and reconcile.

ch11.text: Buying is the mirror image of selling, and it is where most consultants lose credibility, because the client's accountant knows this cycle cold. Start with the purchase order: ten blenders at one hundred twenty, plus ten per cent tax, is one thousand three hundred twenty, and the order moves no stock. The receipt is the document that matters, adding ten units at one hundred twenty and crediting stock received but not billed, an interim account that looks strange and is not an error. The bill clears that account, brings in one hundred twenty of input tax, and creates a creditor of one thousand three hundred twenty with a due date. Then the payment, allocated to the invoice, closes it. Three documents, one quantity, one rate, one total. Teach the learner to predict the tax before looking, and to read the three documents side by side, because that habit is what survives an audit. When a client says the system is wrong, walk this chain in order and the answer appears in one of the four rows.

ch12.text: Suppliers rarely behave the way the process diagram says. They deliver late, send one damaged unit, ask for money before the goods arrive, and send the freight invoice a fortnight afterwards. Each of those has one right document. A return reverses stock first, then the debit note reverses the creditor and the tax, which is why nine units remain at one hundred twenty six each. An advance is money without an invoice, consumed by allocation rather than by a journal, otherwise it sits on the balance sheet forever and the client's auditor asks why. And landed cost is what turns a one hundred twenty rate into a one hundred twenty six valuation, so a two hundred forty sale earns one hundred fourteen rather than one hundred twenty, and the owner's own arithmetic finally agrees with the report. Get those three right and the supplier ageing conversation becomes arithmetic instead of an argument, which is exactly the conversation a distribution client wants to have in week three.

ch13.text: Stock is the part of ERPNext where a small configuration mistake becomes a very large number. Start with the warehouse tree: four leaves, one root, each with the same stock account, because a wrong default account turns every transfer into a valuation difference. A material transfer moves five blenders from main to retail and leaves the total untouched, which is the check to make every single time. Then the stock count. Fifty units on the system, forty seven on the shelf, three units short at one hundred twenty is three hundred sixty of cost, and the reconciliation posts it to a stock adjustment account that finance must recognise. Finally the reorder rule: two units a day for seven days plus ten safety is twenty four, not a round twenty. Set those three things properly and the stock reports stop being arguments, and start being the evidence the client takes to their auditor at the first stock review.

ch14.text: Valuation is where a consultant earns trust, because the owner will check the margin with a calculator. Under FIFO, each receipt creates a layer, and a sale consumes the oldest first. Ten blenders at one hundred twenty and ten at one hundred thirty gives twenty five hundred of stock. Sell twelve and cost of goods sold is one thousand four hundred sixty, leaving eight units worth one thousand forty. That identity, value in equals value out plus value remaining, is the test for every valuation problem. When a rate was wrong or freight arrived late, the answer is a repost item valuation, not a journal entry, and the system will refuse to run it inside a closed period. And negative stock is a decision, not an accident: block it and operations learns to paperwork faster. Decide it, write it down, and the reports stop arguing. Every valuation question ends the same way: show the identity, then show the rows that prove it.

ch15.text: Scanning is the part of stock accuracy that a consultant is asked about most and prepares for least. Start with the barcode data, because one item can carry several codes, including the supplier's own, and a carton code that resolves to twelve units. Then check for duplicates, since two items sharing a code will count wrong in both directions without ever raising an error. Scanning on documents does not create a new kind of transaction: it fills the same rows, so read the totals back before submitting, and demonstrate a refusal rather than letting the floor invent a workaround. Counting is where the money is. Run a blind count so the counter cannot reproduce the expected figure, let the device queue offline, and prove after the sync that the voucher total matches the device total, and that a repeated send is refused. Set the recount threshold in money, name the approver, attach the signed sheet with the device export, and publish a monthly accuracy figure. Finish with the unglamorous part that decides whether any of it survives: label stock, a spare battery, two trained people per shift and a four-page SOP.

ch16.text: Journals are where the accounting primer becomes a daily tool. An accrual records a cost before the invoice arrives, and it must reverse, or February carries January's electricity twice. A prepayment is an asset until the cover is used, so one thousand two hundred of insurance becomes one hundred a month, leaving one thousand one hundred on the balance sheet after the first release. Then the bank. Match every statement line, create the bank charge the ledger is missing, and drive the difference to zero with evidence rather than a plug. And when something was posted to the wrong place, amend it inside the open period or reverse it afterwards. Never delete, because the gap is exactly what an auditor looks for first. Practise the four situations until they are reflexes: accrual, prepayment, bank charge, wrong cost centre. Each one has a canonical remedy, and each remedy leaves a document behind, which is what turns a bookkeeping task into a consulting deliverable.

ch17.text: Month end is a process, not an event, and the consultant who builds the process is the one who gets invited back. Five checks come first: the trial balance, the draft documents, the debtors and creditors control accounts, the bank reconciliation, and stock with tax. When all five are signed, the close can start. January carries twelve thousand of sales, six thousand of cost, and four thousand six hundred eighty of net profit once freight, accrual, insurance and the stock adjustment are counted. The closing voucher moves that to retained earnings and marks the period as reported. At year end the same discipline carries balances into the new year, and the frozen date stops anyone rewriting a year that has already been filed. A close calendar with a name against every task is what makes the process repeatable, and the signed five-page pack is what makes it auditable. Build both once, hand the ownership to the client's finance lead, and the consultant's job becomes review rather than rescue.

ch18.text: Manufacturing scares functional consultants because it looks technical, and it is not. A bill of materials is a recipe: two motors at eighty, one housing at forty, half an hour of assembly at sixty an hour, which gives two hundred thirty per unit. A work order turns demand into a reservation: ten assemblies need twenty motors and ten housings, and nothing has moved yet. The material transfer moves components to the floor, where they are work in progress and still not an expense. Completion consumes the components, adds three hundred of operating cost, and produces ten assemblies at two hundred thirty each. Four documents, one cost, no mystery. If the completion differs from the BOM, check the rate, the time and any extra charges before blaming the system, and write the answer in the production worksheet. A client who can explain a cost per unit from four documents will trust the system with their quotations, and that trust is the whole point of the volume.

ch19.text: Once a client has built something, the next question is what it cost, and the answer has to survive an argument. A completed build of ten assemblies carries two thousand of material and three hundred of labour, so two hundred thirty each, and the entry, the stock ledger and the stock balance must all say the same thing. Scrap is where costing gets real: one unit fails, the total cost does not move, and the nine good units now carry two hundred fifty five fifty six each. Subcontracting adds a bought-in service, twelve ringgit of coating, and a warehouse that must return to zero. Materials, labour, scrap, service: four components, one valuation, and a worksheet that lets the production manager and the accountant argue with numbers instead of opinions. Teach the four components in order, and insist on the worksheet, because a costing conversation without evidence becomes a personality contest, and the consultant is always the outsider in that room.

ch20.text: Services work is deceptively simple, and the margin is where consultants get caught. A project is a cost collector: name it on a timesheet, name it on an invoice, and it carries both sides. Twenty hours at one hundred fifty is three thousand of revenue; twenty hours at eighty is one thousand six hundred of cost; the difference is one thousand four hundred, about forty six per cent. Service tax of eight per cent adds two hundred forty and stays a liability. Record non-billable time anyway, because it costs money even though it cannot be invoiced. Then close the project with a variance note, which is the only way the next quote gets better. A project that is never closed teaches nobody anything and quietly repeats its mistakes. Twenty hours, one rate, one invoice, one margin: when a client can state those four numbers from memory, the services practice is under control, and the next quotation is priced on evidence rather than optimism.

ch21.text: Three modules that clients ask for and rarely operate properly. Fixed assets first: sixty thousand of van becomes twelve thousand a year, one thousand a month, and the register must agree with the control account every month. Quality second: an inspection that rejects one of ten units is the difference between an argument with a supplier and a documented claim. CRM third, and only if somebody owns the pipeline: a lead becomes an opportunity with a value and a probability, twenty four hundred at sixty per cent is fourteen hundred forty, and the quotation is the first document the customer sees. Each module adds a control the client has to run, so sequence them and say plainly what you would leave until year two. Assets and quality carry a control that runs itself once configured; CRM only works when a person owns it, so name that person in the workshop before you switch it on, and put the weekly pipeline review in the same meeting as the sales forecast.

ch22.text: Service work is where a distributor leaks money without noticing, and it starts with the document. A complaint is not a sales return: it is an issue, logged against a serial number, in the customer's words, with a photograph and an owner. Priority comes from impact, and the service level clock follows the priority, which is why working hours and holidays must be configured before anyone promises four hours on a Friday. Warranty is a date, a serial and a condition. Find the delivery date of that exact unit, check the exclusions, and record the decision with its reason, because next year's claim will refer to this one. Then choose the outcome before the work starts: a repair consumes parts and time, a replacement ships a new serial and must take the old one back, a credit closes the commercial complaint. Bill from the issue, so every line names the asset and the visit. And finish with the four numbers the service lead should trust: open issues by priority, median response and resolution, warranty cost against revenue per model, and billable against absorbed hours.

ch23.text: Volume eight is where a functional consultant stops looking like an implementer. Print formats built in the builder give the customer a document worth reading, with the registration and tax number where they belong and totals matching the ledger to the cent. Naming series keep numbering sequential, and a cancelled document keeps its number because reusing one breaks the audit trail. Notifications watch a condition: an order above five thousand emails the sales manager, an order of twelve hundred stays quiet. Letterheads and terms templates make every document look like one company, and they are the easiest handover win because the client can maintain them alone. No code, all configuration, and it all survives the next upgrade. Test five things before handover: one page, matching totals, sequential numbering, one notification above the threshold and silence below it, and a letterhead the client can edit without calling you.

ch24.text: Most requirements a consultant hears can be met in the browser, and the value of knowing where that stops is what this chapter is for. Configuration is anything you can change and reverse in Customize Form: a property setter that renames a label, makes a field mandatory, hides it or makes it read-only, without touching the standard definition underneath. Custom fields come next, but only when somebody will filter, print or report on them, because a field nobody queries is an empty box. Then the DocType editor, where a functional consultant can build a new document with its own naming series and a child table for lines, provided the series is decided before the first record exists. Verify every change the same way: on the form, in the list, under a second role, and again after a migration on staging. Keep a six-column register, with the reason and the reversal, because that is the part the next consultant cannot reconstruct. And when a requirement genuinely needs code, say so plainly, price it, and write the gap down as a decision rather than letting a vague yes carry the project.

ch25.text: Permissions are the least glamorous part of a project and the part that determines whether it survives an audit. Roles follow the org chart, not the software, and the safe default is read, write, create and submit without delete. User permissions restrict a person to their warehouse or territory, and you prove it by logging in as them, because administrators bypass the filter. Then workflow: a discount above ten per cent waits for the sales manager, and the approver is a role so leave does not stop the business. Finally automation, where one wrong template repeats twelve times a year, so review the first cycle. Configure in that order and the client gets control before convenience, and finish with a quarterly access review that the client signs, because a leaver with live access is the finding every audit produces when nobody owns the list, and when nobody has written down who is allowed to do what.

ch26.text: Malaysian tax is the part clients test you on first, because the numbers go to a government portal. Build separate templates for sales tax and service tax, with separate output and input accounts, because the return needs each box separately. Attach item tax templates so the rate follows the product: ten per cent goods, eight per cent services, zero for exempt with a stored certificate. Then the return: twelve hundred output less one hundred twenty input is one thousand eighty payable, and the same three numbers must appear in the tax summary, the ledger and the form. If they do not, the cause is a draft counted, a credit note that did not reverse tax, or a purchase without an input template. Keep the tax advisor's written confirmation with the configuration worksheet, because rates and thresholds change with every budget, and the consultant who documented the basis is the one who gets called back rather than blamed.

ch27.text: e-Invoice is a deadline, not a feature. Everything starts with master data: company and customer TIN, registration, MSIC, address, and a validated TIN before the first submission. When you submit, you get a submission identifier and an accepted list, but accepted only means the portal has the file. Validated is the state that matters, because that is where the UUID and the QR code come from, and that is the legal tax invoice. Cancellation lives inside seventy two hours with a reason, and after that the remedy is a credit note, which the portal enforces with named errors. Consolidate only consumer sales, self-bill only where the rules allow, and give the finance team a daily dashboard routine: clear rejections, cancel what must be cancelled, and confirm nothing is left pending overnight. A monthly tie-out between validated totals and the sales ledger is the check that keeps the project out of trouble.

ch28.text: Migration is where a project is won or lost, and it starts on paper. A mapping workbook with old values, new values and a named owner for every exception is the document the client signs, and it is what ends arguments in month two. Import in dependency order: company, chart of accounts, warehouses and groups, then items, parties and price lists, then users, and only then opening balances. The opening is a journal dated the day before go-live plus a stock reconciliation, and it must balance: ninety six thousand two hundred ninety of assets against three thousand and sixty eight of liabilities and ninety three thousand two hundred twenty two of equity. If it does not balance, the doors stay closed, because every later correction is harder once documents exist. Map on paper, import in order, prove the opening, and only then open the doors to users, with the evidence table signed so the first audit is a page rather than a reconstruction.

ch29.text: The last two weeks decide how the project is remembered. UAT is not a demo: every case states an action and an expected number, five blenders at two hundred forty plus tax is one thousand three hundred twenty, cost six hundred, gross profit six hundred, and the case passes only when those figures appear. Go or no-go is decided on five rows of evidence, with a written acceptance for anything red. Cut-over is a one-page sequence with owners, and the old system stays readable as a rollback position. Then hypercare: five metrics, fifteen minutes, every morning, ending on the date agreed before go-live. Hand over the runbook, the worksheet, the opening pack and the access review, and step back. The measure of a finished engagement is not the invoice, it is a client running their own close, their own UAT for the next change, and their own access review without calling you, because the rhythm lives in their calendar rather than in your notes.

ch30.text: Volume ten ends where most projects are weakest: what happens after go-live, on the day something breaks. Continuity is a consultant deliverable even though the commands belong to somebody else. Pin the versions you went live on and write them in a register. Check with the hosting provider that the nightly backup includes files, and store the site encryption key somewhere the backup cannot reach, because a restored site without its key cannot read what it holds. Then prove it: restore into a scratch site, time it with a stopwatch, log the elapsed minutes with a date and a person, and attach that log to the handover pack. Before every upgrade, restore production data into staging and test there, because print formats, workflows and saved reports break on data and configuration, not just code. Keep one named approver and a cut-off time so a rollback decision takes minutes rather than an argument. Afterwards, twenty minutes of verification: log in as a normal user, submit a test invoice, print it, run two saved reports, and submit one e-Invoice in sandbox. Then sign the ticket and hand the whole section over.

ch31.text: This chapter exists because the site holds the money, and the easiest way in is not technical. Start with accounts: one person one login, no shared warehouse account, and the administrator kept for administration rather than daily invoicing. Write the departure procedure and rehearse it with a test user who holds open documents, because that is the step clients fail under pressure. Then enforce two factor by role, beginning with administrators and finance, after proving that recovery works, so a lost phone is not a lost month end. Privilege is next: withhold delete, restrict by warehouse, and prove it with a second login rather than a configuration screenshot. Network exposure and keys belong to the host and to you jointly, so ask for evidence of a refused connection from outside, keep one key per integration with an owner and a rotation date, and test revocation. Find the encryption key through its named holder without your help. Then sign the one page review, dated, with the items you cannot verify marked as host confirmed. And if something happens, contain access first, preserve the logs second, notify the owner third, and only then restore and verify.

ch32.text: Go live is a launch, not an ending, and the ninety days after it decide whether the client owns a system or rents one. The first week needs a rhythm rather than a hotline: a morning check with a name and a time, same day triage of anything wrong, and one written update every day. Then triage the fix list by consequence. Wrong numbers first, because trust in the ledger is the product, then blocked work, which is usually training or a permission, then the cosmetic items in one agreed batch with a published rule so volume does not decide. At day thirty bring four numbers compared against the go-live baseline, and agree three actions with owners. At day sixty watch a second user, not the champion, complete a weekly cycle unaided, and record every hesitation as a defect rather than a training gap. At day ninety hand over to a named internal owner and a deputy, who can add a user, a warehouse and a print format without calling you. Along the way run the fifteen minute weekly check, prove adoption with counts per role instead of anecdotes, and finish with a dated exit: every item closed, keys handed back, your access revoked, and one optional review priced in writing.
